\section[\texorpdfstring{\mw{लापसी} (lāpsī)}{लापसी (lāpsī)}]{\mw{लापसी} (lāpsī) — a sweet wheat dish}

\label{lesson:MW-C132-lapsi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marwadi for a papad, then the Marwadi for pickle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mw{लापसी}}
\textbf{\mw{लापसी}} — \emph{lāpsī} — \textquotedblleft{}a sweet wheat dish\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mw{लापसी}} (\emph{lāpsī}) is a tadbhava, a word inherited and reshaped by sound change. It comes from \emph{*lappasikā}, \textquotedblleft{}a sweetmeat or dish\textquotedblright{}, a form CDIAL reconstructs from its descendants. CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 10941); the match is through Hindi \emph{lāpsī} and Gujarati \emph{lāpśī}. CDIAL calls Sanskrit \emph{lapsikā} a Sanskritized form of the Middle Indo-Aryan word.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\mw{घेवर} (ghevar)}{घेवर (ghevar)}]{\mw{घेवर} (ghevar) — a honeycomb sweet}

\label{lesson:MW-C132-ghevar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marwadi for pickle, then the Marwadi for a sweet wheat dish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mw{घेवर}}
\textbf{\mw{घेवर}} — \emph{ghevar} — \textquotedblleft{}a honeycomb sweet\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mw{घेवर}} (\emph{ghevar}) is a tadbhava, a word inherited from Sanskrit and reshaped by sound change. It comes from \emph{ghṛtapūra}, \textquotedblleft{}sweetmeat of flour, milk, coconut and ghee\textquotedblright{}. CDIAL gives no Marwari form in this entry (CDIAL 4502); the match is through Gujarati \emph{ghebar}. It is built on \emph{ghṛta}, \textquotedblleft{}ghee\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{pūra}, \textquotedblleft{}cake\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\mw{मक्की} (makkī)}{मक्की (makkī)}]{\mw{मक्की} (makkī) — maize}

\label{lesson:MW-C132-makki}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Marwadi for a sweet wheat dish, then the Marwadi for a honeycomb sweet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mw{मक्की}}
\textbf{\mw{मक्की}} — \emph{makkī} — \textquotedblleft{}maize\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
CDIAL lists Hindi \emph{makkā} and \emph{makāī}, \textquotedblleft{}maize\textquotedblright{}, under Sanskrit \emph{markaka}, the name of a heron-like bird (CDIAL 9879), without explaining the link. Maize reached India from the Americas, so how its name arose is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}
